paragraphs.source_en: Besides, the chills and dizziness had already left my head somewhat muddled, and in my haste to make her quickly grasp the principle that all conditioned things change and all who live must die, I forgot in a flash that she did not understand English, and used it without meaning to. Thinking it over, that was my fault; it was entirely my oversight. Because of this blunder, my chills grew still more violent, and my eyes swam all the more. As for my wife, she followed my instructions: she went to the bathroom, bared her shoulders, put on her makeup, changed into clothes taken from the chest of drawers, and stood ready as though to tell me she could set out at any moment. How anxious I was! I wished Dr. Amaki would come as soon as possible. I looked at the clock; it was already three o'clock. Only one hour remained until four. My wife opened the study door, put her head in, and said, "Shall we be going soon?" It may seem odd to praise one's own wife. To tell the truth, I had never felt my wife so beautiful. Her skin, scrubbed again and again with soap after she had bared her shoulders, looked all the whiter and brighter against her formal black crepe dress. Her face, by the effect of the soap and by her hope of hearing Settsu Daijo, seemed to shine both visibly and invisibly. I felt that, whatever happened, I must go out with her and satisfy that wish. I smoked a cigarette and resolved to go with her. Just then Dr. Amaki arrived, exactly as I had hoped. I told him my symptoms. Dr. Amaki looked at my tongue, took my hand and felt my pulse, tapped my chest, rubbed my back, turned up my eyelids, felt the top of my head, and then thought for a good while. I said, "Somehow I feel it may be rather dangerous." Dr. Amaki calmly replied, "No, I should not think it anything serious." My wife asked, "Excuse me, but would a brief outing be all right?" "Well." Dr. Amaki fell to thinking again. Then he said, "Provided your husband's condition feels..." I immediately said, "It feels quite bad." "Well then, in any case, I shall give you a draught to take in several doses." "Yes, please. Somehow I feel I may be seriously ill." "Not at all. There is no need to worry; it is nothing serious. You must not let your nerves get worked up." With that, he left. By then it was past half past three. So we sent the maid to fetch the medicine. My wife sternly ordered her to run there and run back. When she returned it was a quarter to four, with fifteen minutes still left before four. Until then I had been quite all right, but from that very quarter to four I suddenly began to feel nauseated. My wife poured the medicine into a bowl and set it before me. I picked up the bowl to drink, but from my stomach there suddenly rose a great retching sound, so I had no choice but to put it down. My wife urged me, "You had better drink it quickly." Unless I drank it quickly and set out quickly, I could hardly justify myself. I resolved to drink it down. So I raised the bowl to my lips, and at that moment the retching sound stubbornly interfered again. In this way I lifted the bowl and put it down, put it down and lifted it again. At last the clock in the dining room struck four: clang, clang, clang, clang. Ah, it was already four; I could not dawdle any longer.

paragraphs.source_en: So I picked up the bowl once more. Isn't that strange? I suppose this is precisely what people mean by a strange occurrence. The moment the four o'clock chime sounded, my nausea stopped completely, and I drank the medicine without the slightest difficulty. Then, around ten past four, I truly understood for the first time that Dr. Amaki deserved his reputation as a master physician. The chilly feeling down my back and the spinning in my eyes vanished like a dream. The illness that I had thought might leave me unable to stand for some time was suddenly cured, and I was truly delighted."
